title: The fire of anger
hook: don't be angry, said three times (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, showing off, and your line: not for eyes. Did the hidden good get done, and stay hidden? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

A man comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a simple request. Advise me. Not a question about law, or the end of the world. Just: give me something to carry. The answer is short. Don't be angry. The man asks again, maybe hoping for something bigger. Don't be angry. He asks again. The same answer, every time. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the whole exchange, repetitions and all. Of everything that could have been said, this was the advice. Today's word: ghadab, anger.

First, notice what the advice can't mean. Anger arrives on its own; nobody chooses the first flash. So the hadith is about what happens next. Another hadith in al-Bukhari makes that plain: the strong one isn't the one who throws people in wrestling, but the one who controls himself when he's angry. Strength, moved from the arms to the moment after the flash. Second, the Qur'an praises people who do exactly that. In Pickthall's words, "those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind." Control first, then forgiveness. Anger isn't denied; it's held. Third, the body. Reports in Sunan Abu Dawud give practical steps. If you're angry while standing, sit down; if it hasn't left, lie down. Another report says anger comes from Satan, Satan was made from fire, and fire is put out with water, so when angry, make wudu, the washing before prayer. And in al-Bukhari, when two men were quarreling and one's face had gone red, the Prophet said he knew words that would take it away: seeking refuge in Allah from Satan. Lower the body. Cool the skin. Say the words. Last, why it's called a fire. Fire spreads, and it's hard to call back. What's said in anger tends to outlast the anger. The hadith's short advice gets between the spark and whatever it would catch.
screen: `THE STRONG ONE.` · `THOSE WHO CONTROL THEIR WRATH.` · `SIT, LIE DOWN, MAKE WUDU.` · then, large: `BETWEEN THE SPARK AND WHAT IT CATCHES.`

segments.voice: The practice: when angry, sit or make wudu. Today, rehearse it while calm. Settle into your seat and breathe. Let a small annoyance come to mind, nothing huge: a slow driver, a message left on read. Notice where the heat starts. Chest, face, hands. Now feel the chair under you, holding your weight. You're already doing the first step: sitting. If water is near later, cool your hands and face. If you pray, you can seek refuge in Allah from Satan, as in the hadith. If not, just let the heat cool. The bell holds the time.
Ghadab. Anger; the fire the hadith answers with sitting, water and refuge in Allah. Today's word.

Your line: don't be angry. When the flash comes today, change your position before you open your mouth. Tomorrow, a hunger that doesn't stop: the valley of greed. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to answer anger by sitting or lying down, making wudu, and seeking refuge in Allah from Satan, following hadith reports; restraining anger and forgiving are praised in the Qur'an.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be angry means never feel anger.
what it means: anger comes on its own; the hadith is about what you do next: control, sit, cool it, seek refuge.
what a scholar hears: the repeated advice in al-Bukhari, the strong-man hadith, and Abu Dawud's reports on sitting and wudu, with scholars weighing those reports' chains.
